Scenario:
- Your company has 500 Windows 11 devices that are currently joined to on-premises Active Directory
- The IT team wants to manage these devices using Microsoft Intune
- The devices must retain their existing on-premises AD domain membership for legacy application access
- Users should get single sign-on to both on-premises and cloud resources

Question:
Which device identity configuration should you implement?
choices: Azure AD joined (cloud-only)
Azure AD registered (Workplace joined)
Hybrid Azure AD joined
On-premises AD joined with no Azure AD integration
explanations: Azure AD joined means the device is joined ONLY to Azure AD (Entra ID) — no on-premises AD membership. The requirement explicitly states devices must retain their on-premises AD domain membership for legacy applications. Pure Azure AD join would break that.

Azure AD registered is for personal devices (BYOD). The device is registered with Azure AD but NOT joined to any domain. Users sign in with a local account and add their work account separately. This doesn't maintain on-premises AD membership and isn't suitable for corporate-owned devices requiring domain access.

This option is correct. Hybrid Azure AD join means devices are joined to BOTH on-premises Active Directory AND Azure AD simultaneously. They maintain existing AD domain membership (for legacy apps, Group Policy, network resources) while also being registered in Azure AD (enabling Intune management, Conditional Access, SSO to cloud apps). Azure AD Connect synchronises the device objects. This is the standard migration path for existing domain-joined devices.
Keeping devices on-premises only with no Azure AD integration means Intune cannot manage them. Intune requires Azure AD identity for device enrolment. This option fails the core requirement.
tip: Hybrid Azure AD join = both AD + Azure AD. Best for: existing domain-joined devices migrating to cloud management. Azure AD join = cloud only. Best for: new devices, no on-premises dependency. Azure AD registered = BYOD personal devices. If devices need both on-premises AD AND Intune — Hybrid Azure AD join.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Intune to manage Windows 11 devices
- The security team requires that all managed devices must:
  - Have BitLocker encryption enabled
  - Run a minimum OS version of Windows 11 22H2
  - Have a password with at least 8 characters
- Devices that don't meet these requirements should be marked as non-compliant
- Non-compliant devices should be blocked from accessing Microsoft 365 services

Question:
What TWO things must you configure? (Choose the best single answer that covers both requirements.)
choices: An Intune device compliance policy AND a Conditional Access policy requiring compliant devices
A Group Policy Object (GPO) enforcing BitLocker and password requirements
An Intune device configuration profile with BitLocker settings only
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint device risk policy only
explanations: This option is correct. This requires TWO components working together: (1) An Intune device compliance policy defines what 'compliant' means — BitLocker required, minimum OS version 22H2, minimum password length 8 characters. Intune evaluates each device and marks it compliant or non-compliant. (2) A Conditional Access policy in Azure AD uses the compliance state as a grant condition — 'Require device to be marked as compliant.' Non-compliant devices are blocked from accessing Microsoft 365. Compliance policy defines the rules; Conditional Access enforces access decisions.

Group Policy Objects are for on-premises AD-managed devices. They can enforce settings but don't integrate with Intune compliance evaluation or Conditional Access. GPOs don't mark devices as compliant/non-compliant in Azure AD.

A device configuration profile can deploy BitLocker settings TO a device, but it doesn't evaluate compliance or mark devices as non-compliant. Configuration profiles CONFIGURE devices; compliance policies EVALUATE them. You need a compliance policy to assess the state and Conditional Access to enforce access.

Defender for Endpoint provides device risk scores (low, medium, high) based on threats detected. While risk level can be used in compliance policies, it doesn't evaluate BitLocker, OS version, or password length. It's one input into compliance, not the complete solution.
tip: The compliance + Conditional Access pattern: (1) Compliance policy = DEFINES rules (what must be true). (2) Conditional Access = ENFORCES access (block if non-compliant). They work together. Compliance policy alone = just marks devices. Conditional Access alone = doesn't know what 'compliant' means. You need BOTH.

Scenario:
- Your company is deploying Microsoft 365 Apps to 2,000 managed Windows devices
- Devices are currently on different Office versions (2016, 2019, and some with no Office)
- The IT team wants to:
  - Deploy Microsoft 365 Apps (Current Channel) to all devices
  - Remove all previous Office versions before installing
  - Manage the deployment centrally through Intune

Question:
How should you deploy Microsoft 365 Apps through Intune?
choices: Create a Win32 app package with the Office Deployment Tool and upload to Intune
Use the built-in Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows app type in Intune
Use Windows Autopilot to install Office during OOBE
Download the Office installer and deploy it as a line-of-business (LOB) app
explanations: While you CAN package Office with ODT as a Win32 app, this is unnecessary complexity. Intune has a dedicated, built-in app type specifically for Microsoft 365 Apps that handles the configuration through a guided wizard — no manual packaging needed.

This option is correct. Intune provides a built-in 'Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows' app type. You configure it through a wizard: select the apps to include (Word, Excel, etc.), choose the update channel (Current Channel), set architecture (64-bit), and enable 'Remove other versions of Office' to uninstall Office 2016/2019. Intune handles the download, installation, and removal of previous versions — all centrally managed. This is the Microsoft-recommended approach.

Autopilot runs during the initial device setup (OOBE) for new or reset devices. It doesn't address deploying Office to 2,000 existing devices that are already in use. Autopilot is provisioning, not app deployment to existing devices.

Uploading the Office installer as a LOB app doesn't support the guided configuration options (channel selection, previous version removal, app selection). LOB app type is for simple MSI/MSIX packages, not for complex Office deployments with specific configuration requirements.
tip: Microsoft 365 Apps deployment via Intune: use the dedicated 'Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows' app type (not Win32, not LOB). It provides a configuration wizard for: app selection, update channel, architecture, language, and removal of previous Office versions. This is always the correct exam answer for 'deploy M365 Apps through Intune.'

Scenario:
- Your company wants to automate the deployment of new Windows 11 devices
- When a new employee receives a device, they should:
  - Power on the device and connect to the internet
  - Sign in with their Azure AD credentials
  - Automatically receive company policies, apps, and configurations
- No IT technician should need to touch the device for imaging or setup
- The device should be ready for use within 30 minutes of first power-on

Question:
Which Microsoft service enables this zero-touch provisioning experience?
choices: Windows Autopilot
Microsoft Deployment Toolkit (MDT)
Azure VM Image Builder
System Center Configuration Manager (SCCM/MECM) OSD
explanations: This option is correct. Windows Autopilot is a cloud-based provisioning service. The device's hardware hash is pre-registered in Intune. When a user powers on a new device, it connects to the internet, downloads the Autopilot profile, presents a customised sign-in screen (company branding), and automatically joins Azure AD, enrols in Intune, and receives all assigned policies, apps, and configurations. Zero IT intervention required. The device is shipped directly from the manufacturer to the user.

MDT is an on-premises deployment tool that requires creating and maintaining Windows images, PXE boot infrastructure, and IT technician involvement. It's the traditional imaging approach — the opposite of zero-touch, cloud-driven provisioning.
Azure VM Image Builder creates custom images for Azure Virtual Machines in the cloud. It has nothing to do with provisioning physical Windows devices for end users.

SCCM/MECM Operating System Deployment requires on-premises infrastructure (distribution points, PXE servers, task sequences) and typically involves IT creating and deploying custom Windows images. It's not a zero-touch, cloud-driven solution.
tip: Windows Autopilot = zero-touch, cloud-driven device provisioning. User powers on → signs in → device auto-configures. Key concepts: hardware hash registration, Autopilot profile, self-deploying mode (kiosk), user-driven mode (standard), pre-provisioning (white glove). If the question describes 'zero-touch' or 'cloud provisioning' — Autopilot.

Scenario:
- Your company manages iOS devices with Microsoft Intune
- The security team wants to ensure that:
  - Company data in managed apps (Outlook, Teams, OneDrive) is protected
  - Users cannot copy text from Outlook and paste it into personal apps
  - Company data is wiped from the device if the user leaves the company
  - Personal data on the device must NOT be affected by any IT actions

Question:
Which Intune feature should you configure?
choices: Device configuration profile
App protection policy (MAM)
Device wipe command
Device compliance policy
explanations: Device configuration profiles push settings to devices (Wi-Fi, VPN, email accounts, restrictions). They don't control cut/copy/paste between managed and personal apps or provide app-level data protection.

This option is correct. App protection policies (also called MAM — Mobile Application Management) protect company data at the app level WITHOUT requiring device enrolment. They control: data transfer between managed and unmanaged apps (block copy/paste to personal apps), require PIN to access managed apps, encrypt app data, and enable selective wipe (remove only company data from managed apps, leaving personal data untouched). This is the key feature for protecting corporate data on personal or BYOD devices.

A device wipe command erases the ENTIRE device — including personal photos, apps, and data. The question explicitly requires that personal data must NOT be affected. Device wipe is the nuclear option; app protection policies enable surgical (selective) wipe of company data only.

Device compliance policies evaluate whether a device meets requirements (encryption, PIN, OS version). They don't control data flow between apps or provide selective wipe of company data from managed apps.
tip: App protection policy (MAM) = protect company data WITHOUT device enrolment. Controls: copy/paste, save-as, screenshots between managed/personal apps. Selective wipe = remove only company data. Works on BYOD and enrolled devices. If the question mentions 'protect company data', 'copy/paste restriction', or 'personal data unaffected' — App protection policy.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Windows Autopilot to provision new devices
- A batch of 200 new laptops arrives from the manufacturer
- Before users can enrol these devices via Autopilot, you need to register them
- The manufacturer has provided a CSV file containing the hardware hash for each device

Question:
How do you register these devices for Windows Autopilot?
choices: Import the CSV file containing hardware hashes into Microsoft Intune (or Autopilot service)
Manually join each device to Azure AD through the Settings app
Create an Azure AD dynamic device group based on serial numbers
Install the Intune Company Portal app on each device and sign in
explanations: This option is correct. Import the manufacturer-provided CSV file containing hardware hashes (4K hash) into Microsoft Intune under Devices → Windows enrolment → Devices. Each hardware hash uniquely identifies a device. Once imported, assign an Autopilot deployment profile to these devices. When a user powers on the device and connects to the internet, the Autopilot service recognises the hardware hash and applies the assigned profile. OEMs like Dell, HP, and Lenovo can also register devices directly.

Manually joining each device to Azure AD is Azure AD join, not Autopilot registration. Autopilot requires the device's hardware hash to be registered BEFORE the user turns on the device. Manual Azure AD join happens AFTER the device is running — it's not zero-touch.

Dynamic device groups can organise Autopilot devices AFTER registration (using the ZTDID or order ID attributes), but they don't register devices for Autopilot. Registration is done by importing hardware hashes.

Company Portal is used for user-initiated enrolment of existing devices, not for Autopilot registration. Autopilot requires hardware hash pre-registration — the device needs to be known to the service BEFORE the user touches it.
tip: Autopilot registration = import hardware hashes (CSV) into Intune. Sources: OEM direct registration, partner/reseller upload, manual CSV from Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo script, or manufacturer-provided CSV. The hardware hash (4K hash) uniquely identifies each device. Import FIRST, then assign profiles.

Scenario:
- Your company manages 1,000 Windows 11 devices with Microsoft Intune
- The IT team wants to configure the following on all devices:
  - Wi-Fi profile for the corporate wireless network
  - VPN profile for remote access
  - Email profile for Exchange Online
  - Restrictions (disable camera, block USB storage)

Question:
Which Intune feature should you use to push these settings to devices?
choices: Endpoint security policies
App protection policies
Device compliance policies
Device configuration profiles
explanations: Endpoint security policies focus on security-specific configurations: antivirus, disk encryption (BitLocker), firewall, endpoint detection and response (EDR). While there's overlap with device restrictions, the bulk of the requirements (Wi-Fi, VPN, email) are device configuration profile tasks, not endpoint security.
App protection policies protect data within managed apps (copy/paste, save-as restrictions). They don't configure device-level settings like Wi-Fi, VPN, or hardware restrictions.

Compliance policies EVALUATE whether devices meet requirements (password, encryption, OS version). They don't PUSH settings like Wi-Fi profiles, VPN configurations, or device restrictions. Compliance = assessment. Configuration = deployment of settings.

This option is correct. Device configuration profiles push settings and configurations to managed devices. Profile types include: Wi-Fi (SSID, authentication), VPN (connection settings), Email (Exchange server, authentication), Device restrictions (camera, USB, Bluetooth, screenshots), and many more (certificates, SCEP, PKCS, edition upgrade, custom OMA-URI). You create profiles, assign them to device or user groups, and Intune deploys them automatically.
tip: Intune policy types: Configuration profiles = PUSH settings (Wi-Fi, VPN, email, restrictions). Compliance policies = EVALUATE device state (is it compliant?). App protection = PROTECT data in apps. Endpoint security = SECURE devices (AV, firewall, BitLocker). For 'configure settings on devices' — Device configuration profiles.

Scenario:
- Your company has both Windows and macOS devices managed by Microsoft Intune
- A critical Windows security update was released by Microsoft
- The IT team wants to:
  - Approve the update for deployment to all Windows devices
  - Set a deadline so devices install the update within 5 days
  - Pause updates for a group of test devices if issues are found

Question:
Which Intune feature should you configure for Windows update management?
choices: Feature update policies
Microsoft Store app updates
Win32 app deployment with the update as a package
Windows Update for Business policies (Update rings)
explanations: Feature update policies target a specific Windows feature update version (e.g., Windows 11 23H2) and control which feature update version devices move to. They don't manage monthly security (quality) updates — that's what update rings do.
Microsoft Store app updates manage updates for Store apps. They have nothing to do with Windows OS security updates.

Packaging a Windows security update as a Win32 app is technically possible but completely wrong. Windows updates should be managed through Windows Update for Business, not manually packaged and deployed as applications. This approach would bypass the update infrastructure and create management nightmares.

This option is correct. Windows Update for Business policies (Update rings) in Intune control how and when Windows quality (security) and feature updates are installed. You configure: deferral periods (delay updates by X days), deadline settings (force install within Y days), pause updates (temporarily stop updates for a ring), and maintenance windows. Create separate rings for test/pilot/production groups. Update rings are the primary mechanism for managing Windows security updates through Intune.
tip: Windows update management in Intune: Update rings = quality (security) updates — deferral, deadline, pause. Feature update policies = target specific Windows version. Driver update policies = manage driver updates. Expedite updates = force critical updates immediately. For 'security update management' — Update rings.

Scenario:
- Your company provides virtual desktops to 300 remote workers using Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD)
- Users connect from personal devices that are not managed by Intune
- The IT team wants to optimise the Teams calling experience in AVD sessions
- Users report poor audio and video quality during Teams meetings in their virtual desktops

Question:
Which feature should be enabled to improve Teams performance in AVD?
choices: Install Teams directly on each user's personal device instead
Increase the AVD session host VM size to handle more CPU load
Enable Teams media optimisation (multimedia redirection) for AVD
Configure Azure ExpressRoute for all remote workers
explanations: Installing Teams on personal devices doesn't solve the problem — users need Teams within their AVD session for access to corporate data and integrated workflows. Personal device Teams would be a separate, unmanaged instance without corporate policies.

Increasing VM size adds CPU and memory but doesn't fix the fundamental architecture problem: encoding/decoding video on a remote VM and streaming it as RDP pixels is inherently inefficient. Media optimisation redirects the processing to the local device — a far more effective solution that also reduces VM costs.

This option is correct. Teams media optimisation (also called multimedia redirection) offloads audio/video processing from the AVD session host to the user's local device. Instead of encoding/decoding media streams on the remote VM (consuming CPU and adding latency), the local Teams client handles media directly peer-to-peer. This dramatically improves call quality, reduces latency, and lowers session host resource consumption. It requires the Remote Desktop client (not browser) and the Teams WebSocket service.

ExpressRoute provides private connectivity to Azure, but remote workers connect from home internet. ExpressRoute doesn't extend to individual homes. Even with better network connectivity, the core issue is media processing location, not network path.
tip: AVD Teams optimisation = media redirection to local device. Audio/video processed locally, not on session host. Requires: Remote Desktop client (not browser), WebRTC redirection. This reduces session host CPU and latency. Same concept applies to Citrix HDX and VMware Blast. If the question mentions 'Teams quality in AVD/VDI' — media optimisation.

Scenario:
- Your company wants to provision cloud-based Windows desktops for contractors
- Contractors need a consistent Windows 11 experience with Microsoft 365 Apps
- The IT team wants a predictable per-user monthly cost
- No infrastructure should be managed — no VM sizing, no session host management, no scaling decisions

Question:
Which Microsoft service provides this fully managed cloud PC experience?
choices: Windows 365 Cloud PC
Azure Virtual Machines with Windows 11
Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD)
Microsoft Dev Box
explanations: This option is correct. Windows 365 Cloud PC provides a fully managed, dedicated cloud PC per user. Microsoft handles all infrastructure: provisioning, sizing, patching, scaling, and maintenance. Each user gets their own persistent Windows 11 desktop with Microsoft 365 Apps. Pricing is a simple per-user per-month fee based on the chosen configuration (CPU, RAM, storage). It's a true SaaS Cloud PC — no infrastructure decisions needed.

Azure VMs with Windows 11 require full IaaS management: VM sizing, networking, patching, monitoring, cost management. This is the most management-heavy option and provides variable (not predictable per-user) costs.

AVD requires you to manage session host VMs, choose VM sizes, configure scaling plans, manage images, and plan capacity. It's IaaS/PaaS — you manage the infrastructure. The question explicitly says 'no infrastructure management.' AVD has variable costs based on consumption, not predictable per-user pricing.

Microsoft Dev Box provides cloud-based developer workstations with pre-configured development environments. It's designed for developers, not general contractor use. While similar in concept to Windows 365, it's targeted at dev scenarios with project-based configurations.
tip: Windows 365 = SaaS Cloud PC (fully managed, per-user pricing, predictable cost). AVD = PaaS/IaaS virtual desktops (you manage session hosts, variable cost, multi-session). Key difference: Windows 365 = DEDICATED per-user PC, no infrastructure management. AVD = shared session hosts, more control but more management. If 'predictable per-user cost' + 'no infrastructure' — Windows 365.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft 365 E5 and Exchange Online
- The compliance team discovers that employees are emailing credit card numbers to external recipients
- They want to:
  - Detect emails containing credit card numbers before they are sent
  - Block the email and notify the sender that it violates policy
  - Allow the sender to override the block with a business justification
  - Generate a report of all DLP policy matches

Question:
What should you configure?
choices: Exchange Online mail flow rules (transport rules) to block credit card patterns
Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policy with a rule targeting credit card number sensitive information type
Azure Information Protection sensitivity labels
Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Attachments policy
explanations: Mail flow rules can use regex to detect patterns, but they lack the sophisticated sensitive information type detection (Luhn algorithm validation for credit cards), user override with justification capability, and integrated DLP reporting/dashboard. Transport rules are a basic tool; DLP is the full-featured solution.

This option is correct. Microsoft Purview DLP policies detect sensitive information types (like credit card numbers, using the Luhn algorithm for validation) across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, and endpoints. Configure a DLP rule: condition = 'Content contains credit card number sensitive info type' sent to external recipients, action = block with notification and user override with justification. DLP provides a centralised Activity Explorer and DLP alerts dashboard for reporting. This is the purpose-built solution for this exact scenario.

Sensitivity labels classify and protect documents and emails (encryption, watermarks, headers). Labels don't detect sensitive content patterns like credit card numbers in emails. Labels are applied by users or auto-labelling rules — but the detection and blocking of sensitive data is DLP's job.

Safe Attachments scans email attachments for malware by detonating them in a sandbox. It doesn't detect or block sensitive information like credit card numbers in email body text. It's a threat protection feature, not a data loss prevention feature.
tip: DLP = detect and protect sensitive data (credit cards, SSNs, health records). Works across: Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, Endpoints, Power BI. Key features: sensitive information types, user override with justification, incident reports, Activity Explorer. If the question mentions detecting and blocking sensitive data — DLP.

Scenario:
- Your company is subject to a legal investigation
- The legal team requires that ALL emails and Teams messages for 10 specific employees must be preserved
- No content should be modified or deleted, even if the retention policy would normally delete it
- The preservation must remain in place until the legal team releases it

Question:
Which Microsoft Purview feature should you use?
choices: eDiscovery hold (litigation hold or eDiscovery case hold)
Sensitivity labels with encryption
Retention policy with a 'Retain forever' setting
Data lifecycle management auto-labelling
explanations: This option is correct. An eDiscovery hold (also called litigation hold) preserves ALL content in a user's mailbox and OneDrive indefinitely, regardless of other retention policies or user actions. Content in Recoverable Items cannot be purged. You can place holds on specific custodians (the 10 employees) through an eDiscovery case. The hold remains until explicitly released by the legal team. This is the legally defensible way to preserve data for investigations.

Sensitivity labels classify and protect documents with encryption, watermarks, and access restrictions. They don't preserve content or prevent deletion. Encryption protects confidentiality, not data preservation.

A retention policy with 'Retain forever' applies broadly to locations (all Exchange mailboxes, all SharePoint sites) and is designed for organisational data lifecycle management. It's not targeted to specific users under legal investigation, and it doesn't signal a legal hold that prevents deletion. Users could potentially still purge items from Recoverable Items.
Auto-labelling applies retention labels or sensitivity labels based on content. It's not a hold mechanism for legal investigations. Auto-labelling is a classification tool, not a preservation tool.
tip: eDiscovery hold = legal preservation. Preserves ALL content for specific users, prevents deletion/modification. Types: litigation hold (Exchange) or eDiscovery case hold (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams). Retention policies = organisational lifecycle. If the question mentions 'legal', 'investigation', 'preserve', or 'litigation' — eDiscovery hold.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to protect users from:
  - Phishing emails that contain malicious URLs
  - Emails with weaponised attachments (zero-day malware)
  - Business email compromise (BEC) impersonation attacks

Question:
Which Microsoft 365 security service provides these email threat protection capabilities?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Office 365
Exchange Online Protection (EOP)
Microsoft Defender for Identity
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
explanations: This option is correct. Microsoft Defender for Office 365 (Plan 1 and Plan 2) provides advanced email threat protection beyond EOP: Safe Links (real-time URL scanning and detonation — blocks malicious links at time-of-click), Safe Attachments (sandbox detonation of attachments to detect zero-day malware), Anti-phishing policies with impersonation protection (detects BEC attacks impersonating executives or domains), and Threat Explorer for investigation. Plan 2 adds Threat Trackers, Automated Investigation and Response (AIR), and Attack Simulation Training.

EOP is included with all Exchange Online plans and provides baseline protection: anti-spam, basic anti-malware (known signatures), and mail flow rules. However, EOP does NOT provide advanced threat protection like Safe Links (URL detonation), Safe Attachments (sandbox detonation), or anti-phishing impersonation detection. EOP catches known threats; Defender for Office 365 catches unknown/sophisticated threats.

Defender for Identity monitors on-premises Active Directory signals to detect identity-based attacks (pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, lateral movement). It doesn't protect against email phishing, malicious attachments, or BEC.

Defender for Endpoint protects device endpoints (Windows, macOS, Linux, mobile) against threats — not email. It handles endpoint detection and response (EDR), vulnerability management, and device security. Different protection domain from email.
tip: Microsoft 365 email protection stack: EOP (baseline, all plans) → Defender for Office 365 P1 (Safe Links, Safe Attachments, anti-phishing) → Defender for Office 365 P2 (Threat Explorer, AIR, Attack Simulation). If the question mentions phishing, malicious URLs, zero-day attachments, or impersonation — Defender for Office 365.

Scenario:
- Your company wants to ensure that documents in SharePoint Online are automatically classified and labelled
- Documents containing medical record numbers should be labelled as 'Highly Confidential'
- The label should apply encryption so only users within the organisation can open the document
- External users who receive the document should be unable to open it

Question:
What should you configure?
choices: A sensitivity label with encryption AND an auto-labelling policy that detects medical record numbers
A retention label that marks documents as records
A DLP policy that blocks external sharing of medical records
SharePoint Information Rights Management (IRM) on the document library
explanations: This option is correct. Configure a sensitivity label named 'Highly Confidential' with encryption settings (permissions = organisation members only, external users blocked). Then create an auto-labelling policy that detects the 'medical record number' sensitive information type in SharePoint documents and automatically applies the 'Highly Confidential' label. The label persists with the document — even if downloaded, the encryption follows it. Auto-labelling can work service-side (SharePoint, OneDrive, Exchange) or client-side (Office apps).

Retention labels manage the lifecycle of content (retain for X years, then delete, or declare as a record). They don't classify based on sensitivity, don't apply encryption, and don't restrict access. Retention = lifecycle. Sensitivity = classification and protection.

A DLP policy can detect medical record numbers and block sharing, but it doesn't CLASSIFY documents with a label or apply persistent encryption. DLP prevents data loss; sensitivity labels classify and protect. The question asks for classification AND encryption.

SharePoint IRM protects documents at the library level, but it's a legacy feature being replaced by sensitivity labels. IRM doesn't provide content-based auto-classification (detecting medical records). Sensitivity labels with auto-labelling provide the same protection with intelligent detection.
tip: Sensitivity labels = classify + protect (encryption, watermarks, headers/footers). Auto-labelling = automatically apply labels based on sensitive info types. Retention labels = lifecycle management (retain/delete/record). DLP = detect and block sensitive data sharing. If the question asks for 'classify AND protect' — sensitivity labels.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Azure AD Conditional Access
- The security team wants to block sign-ins from countries where the company has no business operations
- Employees travelling to approved countries should be able to sign in normally
- The policy should apply to all users except the break-glass emergency access account

Question:
Which Conditional Access condition should you configure?
choices: Client app condition filtering by browser type
Device platform condition filtering by operating system
User risk condition from Identity Protection
Named locations condition with countries/regions
explanations: Client app conditions filter by how users authenticate (browser, mobile app, desktop client, legacy auth). They don't evaluate geographic location.

Device platform conditions filter by OS type (Windows, iOS, Android, macOS, Linux). They have nothing to do with geographic location of sign-in attempts. A Windows device can sign in from any country.

User risk evaluates the likelihood that a user account has been compromised (leaked credentials, impossible travel). While impossible travel considers location, user risk is a calculated score — not a configurable list of approved/blocked countries. Named locations provide explicit geographic control.

This option is correct. Named locations in Conditional Access allow you to define trusted and untrusted geographic locations. Create a named location listing the countries where your company operates (approved countries). Then create a Conditional Access policy: condition = 'Any location EXCEPT approved countries', grant = 'Block access', exclude = break-glass account. Sign-ins from non-business countries are blocked; sign-ins from approved countries and the break-glass account proceed normally. Azure AD determines location from the sign-in IP address geolocation.
tip: Conditional Access named locations = geographic access control. Define locations by: countries/regions (IP geolocation) or IP address ranges (trusted office IPs). Common patterns: block sign-ins from non-business countries, require MFA outside office network, trust compliant network locations. If the question mentions geographic restriction — named locations.

stem:
Scenario:
- Your company has 500 Android personal devices (BYOD) used by employees
- The IT team wants to manage ONLY the work profile on these devices
- Corporate apps and data should be in a separate container on the device
- Personal apps and data must be completely untouched by IT

Question:
Which Android enrolment method in Intune supports this requirement?
choices: Android Enterprise work profile (personally-owned)
Android device administrator enrolment
Android Enterprise dedicated device
Android Enterprise fully managed (device owner)
explanations: This option is correct. Android Enterprise work profile (personally-owned) creates a separate, encrypted container on the device for work apps and data. IT manages ONLY the work profile: corporate apps, email, policies. Personal apps, photos, and data remain completely private — IT cannot see or manage them. If the employee leaves, IT can wipe only the work profile. The personal side is untouched. This is the standard BYOD enrolment for Android.

Android device administrator is a legacy enrolment method that Google is deprecating. It gives IT broad device-level control without the clean separation of work and personal data. It's not recommended for BYOD scenarios and doesn't provide the container-based isolation that work profile offers.

Dedicated device mode is for single-purpose, corporate-owned devices (kiosks, digital signage, shared devices). There's no user — the device runs specific apps for a specific purpose. Not applicable to BYOD employee devices.

Fully managed (device owner) gives IT complete control over the entire device — all apps, settings, and data. This is for corporate-owned devices where the company owns the device. It does NOT separate personal and work data because there IS no personal side — IT manages everything.
tip: Android Enterprise enrolment modes: Work profile (personally-owned) = BYOD, separate container. Work profile (corporate-owned) = company device with personal use allowed. Fully managed = company device, IT controls everything. Dedicated = kiosk/single-purpose. If 'BYOD' + 'separate container' + 'personal untouched' — work profile (personally-owned).

stem:
Scenario:
- Your company must retain all emails for 7 years to comply with financial regulations
- After 7 years, emails should be automatically deleted
- The policy must apply to all Exchange Online mailboxes, including new mailboxes created in the future
- No user action should be required — retention should be automatic

Question:
What should you configure in Microsoft Purview?
choices: A retention policy applied to all Exchange mailboxes with 7-year retain-then-delete settings
A retention label published to all mailboxes that users manually apply to emails
Exchange Online mailbox archive with a 7-year archive policy
An eDiscovery hold on all mailboxes for 7 years
explanations: This option is correct. A Microsoft Purview retention policy applied to the Exchange Online location with settings 'Retain items for 7 years, then delete automatically' enforces automatic retention across ALL mailboxes (existing and future). No user action is required — the policy is applied at the organisational level. Items are preserved in place for 7 years (even if users delete them — they go to Recoverable Items). After 7 years, items are permanently deleted. This is the standard approach for regulatory email retention.

Retention labels require user action (manual application) unless auto-apply is configured. Even with auto-apply, labels are item-level (applied to individual emails matching conditions). The question says 'no user action' and 'all emails' — a retention POLICY is the location-wide, automatic approach. Labels are for specific items; policies are for entire locations.

Online Archive (In-Place Archive) moves older emails to an archive mailbox to manage primary mailbox size. It doesn't enforce retention periods or automatic deletion. Archive = storage management. Retention policy = compliance lifecycle management.

eDiscovery holds are for legal investigations and preserve content indefinitely until released. They don't automatically delete after a period. Using eDiscovery holds for routine regulatory retention is a misuse of the feature and creates management overhead.
tip: Retention policies vs retention labels: Policies = automatic, location-wide (all Exchange, all SharePoint), no user action. Labels = item-level, can be manual or auto-applied, more granular. For 'apply to everything automatically' — retention POLICY. For 'classify specific items differently' — retention LABELS. Both can retain-then-delete.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Intune to manage devices
- The security team wants to deploy BitLocker encryption to all Windows 11 devices
- BitLocker recovery keys must be stored in Azure AD for IT support access
- The encryption should be enforced silently without user interaction

Question:
How should you deploy BitLocker through Intune?
choices: Use a PowerShell script deployed through Intune to run manage-bde commands
Create an Intune endpoint security disk encryption policy for BitLocker
Create an Intune device configuration profile with a BitLocker template
Deploy BitLocker through Group Policy and wait for Hybrid Azure AD sync
explanations: PowerShell scripts for BitLocker are unnecessarily complex and don't provide the managed policy experience. Recovery key escrow to Azure AD wouldn't be handled natively. Scripts run once; policies continuously evaluate and enforce.

This option is correct. Intune endpoint security policies include a dedicated Disk encryption profile type for BitLocker. Configure: silent encryption (no user interaction required — works on modern TPM 2.0 devices with Azure AD join), recovery key escrow to Azure AD (stored automatically — IT can retrieve via Azure AD or Intune portal), encryption method (XTS-AES 256), and which drives to encrypt. This is the Microsoft-recommended approach for managing BitLocker through Intune. Recovery keys are automatically backed up to Azure AD.

A device configuration profile with the Endpoint protection template CAN configure BitLocker, but Intune has since introduced dedicated endpoint security policies specifically for disk encryption. The endpoint security approach provides a more focused, cleaner configuration experience with all BitLocker settings in one place. Microsoft recommends using endpoint security policies for security configurations.

Group Policy is for on-premises AD environments and doesn't back up recovery keys to Azure AD natively. For Intune-managed devices, use Intune policies. Hybrid scenarios add unnecessary complexity when Intune endpoint security policies handle it directly.
tip: BitLocker through Intune: use Endpoint security → Disk encryption policy. Key settings: silent encryption (no user prompt), recovery key escrow to Azure AD, XTS-AES 256-bit. Silent encryption requires: TPM 2.0, UEFI, Azure AD joined (or Hybrid), no pre-provisioned OS volume. Recovery keys viewable in Azure AD and Intune device properties.

Scenario:
- Your company has Microsoft 365 E5 licenses
- The security team discovers suspicious sign-in activity:
  - A user signed in from London at 9:00 AM
  - The same user signed in from Tokyo at 9:30 AM (impossible travel)
  - The sign-in from Tokyo used a legacy authentication protocol
- The security team wants automatic detection and response to these types of threats

Question:
Which Microsoft service automatically detects impossible travel and risky sign-in behaviour?
choices: Azure AD Conditional Access
Azure AD Identity Protection
Microsoft Sentinel
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
explanations: Conditional Access enforces access policies based on conditions (location, device, risk level), but it doesn't DETECT impossible travel or calculate risk scores. Conditional Access consumes risk information from Identity Protection — it doesn't generate it. It's the enforcement engine, not the detection engine.

This option is correct. Azure AD Identity Protection uses machine learning to detect risky sign-in behaviours including: impossible travel (signing in from geographically distant locations in impossible time), anonymous IP address use, malware-linked IP addresses, unfamiliar sign-in properties, and legacy authentication from unusual locations. It calculates sign-in risk (low, medium, high) and user risk. You can configure automated responses: require MFA for medium risk, block sign-in for high risk, require password change for compromised users.

Microsoft Sentinel is a SIEM/SOAR platform that aggregates security data from multiple sources for threat detection and incident response. It can ingest Identity Protection alerts but doesn't perform the primary detection of impossible travel — that's Identity Protection's role.

Defender for Cloud Apps (formerly Cloud App Security) is a CASB that monitors cloud app usage, detects shadow IT, and provides threat detection across SaaS applications. While it has anomaly detection, Identity Protection is the purpose-built service for Azure AD sign-in risk and impossible travel detection.
tip: Identity Protection = detect risky sign-ins and compromised users. Risk types: impossible travel, anonymous IP, unfamiliar properties, leaked credentials. Risk levels: low, medium, high. Automated responses: require MFA, block, force password change. Conditional Access CONSUMES risk signals from Identity Protection. If 'detect risky sign-in' — Identity Protection.

Scenario:
- Your company wants to deploy a custom line-of-business (LOB) Windows application to managed devices
- The application is packaged as an MSI installer
- The app must be installed silently without user interaction
- You want to track installation success and failure through Intune

Question:
Which Intune app type should you use?
choices: Microsoft Store app (new)
Web link
Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows
Windows app (Win32)
explanations: Microsoft Store app (new) deploys apps from the Microsoft Store or private store. A custom LOB MSI installer is not in the Microsoft Store. This app type is for Store-published applications only.
A web link creates a shortcut to a URL — it doesn't install a native Windows application. It's for web-based apps and bookmarks, not MSI installer packages.
Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows is a dedicated app type specifically for deploying the Office suite. It's not for custom LOB applications.

This option is correct. The Win32 app type in Intune handles MSI, EXE, and MSIX packages for Windows applications. You wrap the MSI with the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool (IntuneWinAppUtil.exe) to create a .intunewin package, upload it to Intune, configure silent install commands (msiexec /i app.msi /qn), detection rules (MSI product code, file existence, or registry key), and dependencies. Intune tracks installation status (installed, failed, pending) in the device install status report.
tip: Intune app types for Windows: Win32 = MSI/EXE/MSIX (most flexible, detection rules, dependencies, requirements). LOB = simple MSI/APPX without Win32 wrapping. Store app = Microsoft Store apps. M365 Apps = Office suite only. For custom LOB applications — Win32 app type is the recommended approach.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Intune to manage devices
- The IT team wants to deploy apps with the following assignment types:
  - Required apps: automatically installed on all devices in the assigned group
  - Available apps: users can choose to install from the Company Portal
  - Uninstall: removes the app from all devices in the assigned group
- They assign a LOB app as 'Required' to the Sales group and 'Available' to the Marketing group

Question:
What happens for a user who is in BOTH the Sales and Marketing groups?
choices: The app is automatically installed (Required) — Required takes precedence over Available
A conflict occurs and the app is not deployed to the user
The app appears as Available in the Company Portal — the user can choose to install it
The user is prompted to choose between Required and Available installation
explanations: This option is correct. When a user is targeted by both Required and Available assignments for the same app, Intune applies the most restrictive (strongest) intent. The precedence order is: Uninstall > Required > Available. Since Required is stronger than Available, the app is automatically installed. The user doesn't get a choice — the Required assignment wins. This conflict resolution is handled automatically by Intune.
Intune does not create conflicts for overlapping assignment types — it resolves them using intent precedence. No deployment failure occurs.

Available means optional — the user can install from Company Portal if they want. But since the user is also in the Sales group where the app is Required, Intune enforces the Required assignment. Required is a stronger intent than Available.
Intune doesn't prompt users to resolve assignment conflicts. The precedence rules are applied automatically.
tip: Intune app assignment precedence: Uninstall > Required > Available. If a user is in multiple groups with different assignment types, the strongest intent wins. Required + Available = Required (auto-install). Required + Uninstall = Uninstall (removed). No user choice in conflicts — Intune resolves automatically.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft 365 and wants to implement the Zero Trust security model
- The CISO asks: 'What are the core principles of Zero Trust that we should follow?'

Question:
Which set of principles defines the Zero Trust model?
choices: Trust the internal network, verify external access, use firewalls
Verify explicitly, use least privilege access, assume breach
Encrypt everything, use VPNs, trust verified users indefinitely
Block all external access, allow only internal access, use on-premises security
explanations: Trusting the internal network is the OPPOSITE of Zero Trust. Zero Trust eliminates the concept of a trusted internal network — every access request is verified regardless of network location. This is the traditional perimeter-based security model that Zero Trust replaces.

This option is correct. Zero Trust is built on three core principles: (1) Verify explicitly — always authenticate and authorise based on all available data points (identity, location, device health, service, data, anomalies). (2) Use least privilege access — limit user access with just-in-time and just-enough-access (JIT/JEA), risk-based adaptive policies, and data protection. (3) Assume breach — minimise blast radius, segment access, verify end-to-end encryption, use analytics for detection and response.

VPNs and trusting users indefinitely contradict Zero Trust. Zero Trust doesn't trust any user indefinitely — every access is continuously verified. VPNs are a perimeter-based tool; Zero Trust works regardless of network location.

Blocking all external access is impractical for modern cloud-based organisations using SaaS services. Zero Trust enables secure access from anywhere by verifying every request — it doesn't block access based on location.
tip: Zero Trust principles: (1) Verify explicitly (always authenticate, use all signals). (2) Least privilege access (JIT/JEA, just enough permissions). (3) Assume breach (minimise blast radius, segment, detect). Microsoft implements Zero Trust through: Azure AD, Conditional Access, Intune, Defender, Purview. This is a common exam topic.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft 365 and Azure AD
- The Global Administrator account has been compromised
- The attacker has:
  - Changed the admin password
  - Added their own MFA method
  - Created new admin accounts
  - Modified Conditional Access policies

Question:
Which emergency access mechanism should have been in place to recover from this scenario?
choices: Break-glass emergency access accounts excluded from Conditional Access
Azure subscription owner account with Azure AD management rights
Azure AD Connect with on-premises AD admin fallback
Microsoft support ticket to reset the Global Admin password
explanations: This option is correct. Break-glass (emergency access) accounts are highly privileged Azure AD accounts specifically designed for emergency scenarios when normal admin accounts are compromised or locked out. Best practices: at least 2 break-glass accounts, excluded from ALL Conditional Access policies (including MFA requirements), cloud-only (no on-premises sync), not assigned to any individual, passwords stored securely offline (safe/vault), monitored with alerts for any sign-in activity. These accounts let you regain control of Azure AD even when all other admin accounts are compromised.

Azure subscription owner and Azure AD Global Admin are separate roles. Subscription owner manages Azure resources (VMs, storage), not Azure AD (users, policies, Conditional Access). They can't reset Azure AD admin passwords or modify Conditional Access policies.

Azure AD Connect synchronises on-premises AD to Azure AD, but on-premises admin accounts don't automatically have Azure AD Global Admin privileges. If the attacker has modified Azure AD directly, on-premises AD admin access doesn't help recover Azure AD control. They're separate admin planes.

While Microsoft support can assist, it's a slow process with identity verification requirements. By the time support resolves it, the attacker has had extended access. Break-glass accounts provide immediate, self-service recovery.
tip: Break-glass accounts: 2 cloud-only accounts, Global Admin role, excluded from ALL Conditional Access, strong passwords stored offline, monitored with Azure Monitor alerts. NEVER use for daily admin work. Test periodically. If the question mentions emergency access or admin lockout recovery — break-glass accounts.

Scenario:
- Your company deploys Microsoft 365 Apps to 1,500 devices
- The IT team wants to:
  - Deploy the Monthly Enterprise Channel for stability
  - Exclude Access and Publisher from the installation
  - Include the Microsoft Teams desktop app
  - Use 64-bit architecture

Question:
Where do you configure these installation settings when deploying through Intune?
choices: In the Microsoft 365 admin centre Apps settings page
In the Office Customization Tool (OCT) and deploy via SCCM
In a PowerShell script that runs the Office Deployment Tool with a configuration.xml
In the Intune Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows app configuration (App suite information and settings)
explanations: The Microsoft 365 admin centre manages organisation-wide settings (update channel defaults, feature access), but it doesn't handle per-device deployment configuration through Intune. The app deployment settings are configured within Intune itself.

The OCT and SCCM are for on-premises deployment. Intune is a cloud management tool and doesn't use SCCM deployment infrastructure. While you can use ODT with configuration.xml for manual deployments, Intune has a built-in wizard for this.

While PowerShell with ODT and configuration.xml works for manual deployments, Intune provides a native GUI-based configuration experience. Using PowerShell scripts bypasses Intune's deployment tracking, reporting, and assignment capabilities.

This option is correct. When you add a 'Microsoft 365 Apps for Windows' app in Intune, the configuration wizard lets you specify all these settings through the UI: select apps to include/exclude (remove Access and Publisher), choose update channel (Monthly Enterprise Channel), select architecture (64-bit), include Teams, set language, and configure other options. These settings are configured in the 'App suite information' and 'App suite settings' tabs during app creation. No manual XML editing required.
tip: Microsoft 365 Apps deployment via Intune wizard: App suite information (name, description) → App suite settings (products to include/exclude, update channel, architecture, language, Teams). All configurable through the Intune UI. The wizard generates the ODT configuration behind the scenes. If 'deploy M365 Apps through Intune' — use the built-in app type wizard.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on all Windows devices
- A suspicious file is detected on a device and Defender for Endpoint flags it as malicious
- The security analyst wants to:
  - Isolate the affected device from the network
  - Collect an investigation package (forensic data)
  - Run an antivirus scan on the device
- All actions should be performed remotely without physical access to the device

Question:
Where does the security analyst perform these response actions?
choices: Microsoft Defender portal — device page response actions
Microsoft Intune device actions (remote wipe, retire)
Exchange Online admin centre — mobile device management
Azure AD admin centre — device management
explanations: This option is correct. The Microsoft Defender portal (security.microsoft.com) provides response actions on the device page: Isolate device (cut network access while maintaining Defender connectivity for remote management), Collect investigation package (gathers forensic data — running processes, network connections, registry, event logs), Run antivirus scan (trigger Microsoft Defender Antivirus remotely), Restrict app execution (block unsigned processes), Initiate automated investigation, and Initiate Live Response (remote shell). All done remotely through the portal.

Intune device actions include remote wipe, retire, restart, and sync. These are device management actions, not security investigation and response actions. Intune doesn't provide network isolation, forensic investigation packages, or targeted antivirus scans for security incidents.
Exchange Online MDM manages mobile device access to Exchange. It has basic wipe capabilities but no advanced security investigation or response features.
Azure AD admin centre manages device identity (registered, joined, compliant status). It doesn't provide security response actions like network isolation, forensic collection, or antivirus scanning.
tip: Defender for Endpoint response actions: Isolate device (network isolation), Collect investigation package (forensics), Run AV scan, Restrict app execution, Live Response (remote shell), Automated investigation. All in Microsoft Defender portal → Device page → Response actions. Different from Intune device actions (management, not security response).

Scenario:
- Your company manages Windows 11 devices with Microsoft Intune
- An Intune device configuration profile and a Group Policy Object (GPO) both configure the same setting
- The GPO sets the screen lock timeout to 15 minutes
- The Intune profile sets the screen lock timeout to 5 minutes
- The device is Hybrid Azure AD joined

Question:
Which setting takes effect on the device?
choices: The GPO setting (15 minutes) — GPO always wins over Intune
The conflict depends on the specific CSP — by default, MDM (Intune) wins over GPO on Windows 10/11 Azure AD-joined devices
Both settings are applied and the device alternates between them
The Intune setting (5 minutes) — Intune always wins over GPO
explanations: GPO does NOT always win over Intune. On Windows 10/11, Microsoft introduced a policy resolution mechanism that gives MDM (Intune) precedence over GPO for co-managed or Azure AD-joined devices. The traditional 'GPO wins' behaviour only applies in purely on-premises AD environments.

This option is correct. On Windows 10/11 devices that are Azure AD joined or Hybrid Azure AD joined with MDM enrolment, the ControlPolicyConflict CSP determines which policy source wins when both GPO and MDM configure the same setting. By default, MDM (Intune) takes precedence over GPO. This means the 5-minute timeout from Intune is applied. This behaviour can be changed by configuring the MDMWinsOverGP policy. This is critical to understand during GPO-to-Intune migration.
Devices don't alternate between conflicting settings. Windows applies one setting based on the policy precedence rules. Conflicting policies are resolved, not merged.

While MDM wins by default on Azure AD-joined devices, saying 'Intune always wins' is an oversimplification. The behaviour can be configured using the ControlPolicyConflict/MDMWinsOverGP CSP. The correct answer acknowledges the MDM precedence mechanism.
tip: GPO vs Intune conflict resolution: MDMWinsOverGP CSP controls precedence. Default on Azure AD/Hybrid joined: MDM (Intune) wins. This is by design for cloud-first management. During migration, use Intune Settings Catalog to find matching settings and retire GPOs gradually. Exam favourite: 'What happens when GPO and Intune conflict?' — MDM wins by default.

Scenario:
- Your company wants to classify and protect email messages based on their content
- The legal team sends emails containing attorney-client privileged information
- These emails should be automatically:
  - Labelled as 'Attorney-Client Privilege'
  - Encrypted so only the sender and recipients can read them
  - Prevented from being forwarded to anyone

Question:
Which Microsoft Purview feature should you configure?
choices: Communication compliance policy
Sensitivity label with encryption and rights management (Do Not Forward)
Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policy for Exchange
Retention label with 'Mark as regulatory record'
explanations: Communication compliance monitors communications for policy violations (harassment, insider trading, regulatory compliance). It doesn't classify, encrypt, or apply forwarding restrictions to emails.

This option is correct. A sensitivity label named 'Attorney-Client Privilege' with encryption settings: user-defined permissions or 'Do Not Forward' rights management. Do Not Forward prevents recipients from forwarding, printing, or copying the email. The label can be applied manually by the legal team or auto-applied using keyword/sensitive info type detection. The encryption persists with the email — even if forwarded (if allowed), only authorised recipients can read it.

DLP detects and can block sensitive content, but it doesn't classify emails with labels or apply persistent encryption with rights management. DLP prevents data from leaving — it doesn't protect data with encryption and forward restrictions.

Retention labels manage content lifecycle (retain/delete). They don't encrypt content or prevent forwarding. Regulatory records prevent content from being edited or deleted, but that's about lifecycle immutability, not confidentiality protection.
tip: Sensitivity labels with encryption rights: Do Not Forward = recipients can read but NOT forward, print, or copy. Encrypt-Only = recipients can read and forward but not modify permissions. Custom permissions = granular rights (view, edit, print, forward). If 'prevent forwarding' + 'encrypt' — sensitivity label with Do Not Forward.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Intune and has the following device groups:
  - Group A: All Windows devices (dynamic membership rule: deviceOS = Windows)
  - Group B: Finance department devices (manually assigned)
  - Group C: All company devices (All devices built-in group)
- A compliance policy requiring a 6-character PIN is assigned to Group A
- A compliance policy requiring an 8-character PIN is assigned to Group B
- A Finance department Windows device is in both Group A and Group B

Question:
What PIN length is required for the Finance department Windows device?
choices: 6 characters (the less restrictive setting wins to avoid user impact)
8 characters (the most restrictive setting wins)
6 characters (Group A policy wins because it was assigned first)
The device is marked as non-compliant due to the conflict
explanations: Intune does NOT apply the least restrictive setting for compliance policies. Security-related settings always resolve to the most restrictive value to maintain security posture. Applying the less restrictive value would create a security gap.

This option is correct. When multiple compliance policies target the same device with conflicting settings, Intune applies the most restrictive (most secure) value. A device in both Group A (6-char PIN) and Group B (8-char PIN) must meet the 8-character PIN requirement because it's more restrictive. This ensures security is never weakened by overlapping policy assignments. The device must satisfy ALL assigned policies.

Assignment order doesn't determine which policy wins in Intune. Intune doesn't process policies in a queue — it evaluates all assigned policies and applies conflict resolution rules based on the setting values.

Conflicting compliance policies don't automatically mark devices as non-compliant. Intune resolves numeric conflicts by applying the most restrictive value. The device is evaluated against the resolved settings.
tip: Intune compliance policy conflicts: most restrictive value wins for numeric settings (longer PIN, newer OS version). For boolean settings (require encryption: yes vs no): 'yes' wins. This ensures maximum security. Different from configuration profile conflicts where the last-applied may win or create errors. Compliance = most restrictive always.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Intune to manage iOS devices
- The IT team wants to prevent users from installing apps from the Apple App Store that are not approved by IT
- Only apps deployed through Intune or the Company Portal should be available
- Users should not be able to browse or download apps from the public App Store

Question:
How should you restrict App Store access on managed iOS devices?
choices: Create an App protection policy that blocks the App Store
Create a Conditional Access policy that blocks access to the App Store
Create a device configuration profile with device restrictions that block the App Store app
Uninstall the App Store app from all devices using a PowerShell script
explanations: App protection policies (MAM) protect data within managed apps. They don't control which apps can be installed or block access to the App Store. MAM operates at the app data level, not the device configuration level.

Conditional Access controls access to cloud services based on conditions (user, device, location, risk). The Apple App Store is not an Azure AD-integrated cloud service — Conditional Access cannot block it. App Store access is controlled at the device configuration level.

This option is correct. An Intune device configuration profile with iOS/iPadOS device restrictions can block the App Store. Under 'Built-in Apps' restrictions, disable 'Allow App Store'. This hides the App Store from the device, preventing users from browsing or downloading unapproved apps. IT can still push apps through Intune (VPP/ABM apps or Store apps managed through Intune). This requires supervised iOS devices for full restriction enforcement.

You cannot uninstall the App Store from iOS — it's a system app. Even on supervised devices, you can only hide it through device restrictions, not uninstall it. PowerShell doesn't run natively on iOS devices.
tip: iOS device restrictions in Intune: block App Store, block camera, block screenshots, restrict AirDrop, disable iCloud backup, require managed pasteboard, and more. IMPORTANT: Many iOS restrictions require SUPERVISED mode (Apple Business Manager + automated device enrolment). If 'block App Store on iOS' — device restriction profile (supervised mode).

Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft 365 E5
- The security team wants to investigate and respond to advanced threats across:
  - Email (phishing, malicious attachments)
  - Endpoints (malware, exploits)
  - Identity (compromised accounts, lateral movement)
  - Cloud apps (shadow IT, suspicious activity)
- They want a single portal that correlates alerts from all these sources into unified incidents

Question:
Which Microsoft security solution provides this unified cross-domain threat detection and response?
choices: Microsoft 365 Defender (now Microsoft Defender XDR)
Microsoft Defender for Office 365 only
Azure Security Centre only
Microsoft Sentinel only
explanations: This option is correct. Microsoft 365 Defender (rebranded as Microsoft Defender XDR — Extended Detection and Response) correlates alerts from: Defender for Office 365 (email), Defender for Endpoint (devices), Defender for Identity (on-premises AD), and Defender for Cloud Apps (SaaS apps). It automatically correlates related alerts into unified incidents, enabling security teams to see the full attack chain across domains. The unified portal (security.microsoft.com) provides incident investigation, automated investigation and response (AIR), and advanced hunting with KQL.

Defender for Office 365 covers only email and collaboration threats (phishing, malicious attachments, Safe Links). It doesn't provide endpoint protection, identity threat detection, or cloud app security. It's one component of the broader Defender suite.

Azure Security Centre (now Microsoft Defender for Cloud) focuses on cloud infrastructure security (Azure VMs, containers, SQL, storage). It doesn't cover email, endpoint, or identity threats in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem.

Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM/SOAR that can ingest data from Microsoft 365 Defender AND third-party sources. While Sentinel provides broader security analytics, the question asks about cross-domain Microsoft 365 threat detection and correlation — that's XDR's purpose. Sentinel is complementary (SIEM), not the XDR layer itself.
tip: Microsoft Defender XDR = unified cross-domain threat detection and response. Correlates: Defender for Office 365 (email) + Defender for Endpoint (devices) + Defender for Identity (identity) + Defender for Cloud Apps (SaaS). Single portal: security.microsoft.com. Sentinel = SIEM/SOAR (broader, includes third-party data). XDR + Sentinel = complete security operations.

stem:
Scenario:
- Your company uses Microsoft Endpoint Manager (Intune) and Configuration Manager (MECM)
- Currently, devices are managed by MECM with on-premises infrastructure
- The IT team wants to gradually shift management workloads to Intune while keeping MECM for specific tasks
- During the transition, some workloads should be managed by Intune and others by MECM

Question:
Which feature enables this gradual transition between MECM and Intune?
choices: Hybrid Azure AD join
Tenant attach
Azure AD Connect
Co-management
explanations: Hybrid Azure AD join enables devices to be in both on-premises AD and Azure AD simultaneously. It's a prerequisite for co-management but doesn't itself control which management tool handles which workloads. Hybrid join is about device identity, not workload management.

Tenant attach uploads MECM device data to the Intune portal for visibility and limited remote actions, but it doesn't split management workloads between the two tools. Tenant attach is 'view MECM devices in the cloud'; co-management is 'manage devices with both tools simultaneously.'

Azure AD Connect synchronises on-premises AD identities to Azure AD. It's an identity sync tool, not a device management workload migration tool. It's a prerequisite for cloud identity but doesn't control which management platform handles device policies.

This option is correct. Co-management allows devices to be simultaneously managed by BOTH Configuration Manager AND Intune. You can slide individual workloads between them: compliance policies, device configuration, Windows Update, resource access, endpoint protection, Office apps, and client apps. Each workload has a slider: MECM ← → Intune. This enables a gradual, workload-by-workload migration from MECM to Intune without disrupting device management.
tip: Co-management = dual management (MECM + Intune) with workload sliders. Workloads you can shift: compliance, device config, Windows Update, resource access, endpoint protection, Office apps, client apps. Tenant attach = see MECM devices in Intune portal (visibility). Co-management = actually manage them from either tool (control). Different concepts!

stem:
Scenario:
- Your company has Microsoft 365 E5
- The compliance team needs to search for specific emails across all employee mailboxes
- They received a regulatory request to find all emails containing the phrase 'Project Phoenix'
- The search results must be exportable for legal review
- Only compliance officers should be able to perform these searches

Question:
Which Microsoft Purview feature should the compliance team use?
choices: Audit log search in the Microsoft Purview portal
Microsoft Purview eDiscovery (Standard or Premium)
Content search in Microsoft Purview
Data classification in Microsoft Purview
explanations: Audit log search shows WHO did WHAT in Microsoft 365 (user activities, admin actions). It doesn't search email content or mailbox data. Audit logs record events like 'User A signed in' or 'Admin B deleted a mailbox rule' — not email body text.

This option is correct. Microsoft Purview eDiscovery (Standard) provides: content search across all mailboxes, cases for organising investigations, holds to preserve relevant data, search results review and export for legal counsel, and role-based access (eDiscovery Manager role). eDiscovery Premium adds: custodian management, advanced processing, review sets with analytics (threading, near-duplicate detection), and predictive coding. For regulatory/legal content searches — eDiscovery is the appropriate tool with proper audit trails and access controls.

Content search can search across mailboxes, SharePoint, and OneDrive for specific content. However, it lacks the case management, hold capabilities, and review set features needed for legal/regulatory processes. For regulatory requests, eDiscovery provides the proper workflow.

Data classification scans and identifies sensitive information types across Microsoft 365 content. It classifies content (credit cards, SSNs, medical records) but doesn't provide searchable content discovery, case management, or export for legal review.
tip: eDiscovery = legal/regulatory content search, hold, and export. Content search = basic cross-service search (subset of eDiscovery). eDiscovery Standard = cases, holds, search, export. eDiscovery Premium = custodians, review sets, analytics, predictive coding. Required role: eDiscovery Manager or eDiscovery Administrator. If 'legal', 'regulatory', or 'export for review' — eDiscovery.

stem:
Scenario:
- Your company purchases iOS apps in bulk through Apple Business Manager (ABM)
- 200 licences of a paid app have been purchased
- The IT team wants to:
  - Distribute the app to managed iOS devices through Intune
  - Revoke and reassign licences when employees leave the company
  - Deploy the app without requiring users to have personal Apple IDs

Question:
Which Intune feature supports this app distribution model?
choices: iOS app configuration policy
Managed Google Play (Android Enterprise)
Volume Purchase Program (VPP) / Apple Business Manager app sync with Intune
Apple App Store link in Intune
explanations: iOS app configuration policies push configuration settings (key-value pairs, XML) to apps AFTER they're installed. They don't handle app distribution, licensing, or deployment. App config = configure app settings, not install apps.
Managed Google Play is the Android Enterprise app distribution mechanism. It has nothing to do with iOS app distribution — that's handled through Apple Business Manager.

This option is correct. Apple Business Manager (ABM) — formerly Volume Purchase Program (VPP) — allows organisations to purchase iOS/macOS apps in bulk. When you sync ABM with Intune, purchased app licences appear in Intune. You can then assign apps to devices (device licensing — no Apple ID needed) or users (user licensing — Apple ID required). When an employee leaves, Intune automatically revokes the licence, making it available for reassignment. This is the proper enterprise iOS app distribution model.

Adding an App Store link in Intune creates a pointer to the public App Store. Users need their own Apple ID and must purchase/download the app themselves. IT cannot manage licences, revoke assignments, or track licence usage. This doesn't support volume-purchased apps.
tip: Apple Business Manager (ABM) + Intune: purchase apps in bulk, sync licences to Intune, assign to devices (no Apple ID needed) or users. Licence revocation = automatic when unassigned. Device-based licensing = the app installs without any Apple ID. If 'volume iOS apps' + 'revoke/reassign licences' — ABM/VPP sync with Intune.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Windows Autopilot with user-driven deployment mode
- A new employee joins and receives a laptop
- During the Autopilot OOBE (Out of Box Experience), the device:
  1. Connects to the internet
  2. Identifies itself via hardware hash
  3. Downloads the Autopilot profile
  4. Presents the company-branded sign-in page
  5. The user signs in with their Azure AD credentials

Question:
What happens AFTER the user signs in during Autopilot user-driven deployment?
choices: The device is manually imaged by IT with a corporate Windows image
The device reboots into Windows Setup for a fresh OS installation
The device joins Azure AD (or Hybrid Azure AD), enrols in Intune, and receives assigned policies, apps, and configurations
The user must manually enrol the device in Intune through the Company Portal
explanations: Autopilot does NOT require imaging. The device ships with Windows pre-installed from the manufacturer. Autopilot configures the existing Windows installation — it's cloud-driven provisioning, not traditional imaging. No IT intervention needed.

Autopilot doesn't reinstall Windows. It transforms the factory OEM Windows installation into a corporate-configured device through cloud-driven policy application. No OS reinstallation, no rebooting into setup.

This option is correct. After the user signs in: the device automatically joins Azure AD (or Hybrid Azure AD based on the Autopilot profile), automatically enrols in Microsoft Intune (MDM), Intune pushes all assigned device configuration profiles, compliance policies, apps (M365 Apps, LOB apps), security baselines, and endpoint security policies. The user sees an Enrolment Status Page (ESP) showing installation progress. Once complete, the desktop appears fully configured. The entire process is automated — zero IT intervention.
Autopilot user-driven mode automatically enrols the device in Intune after Azure AD join — there's no manual Company Portal enrolment step. The device is enrolled during the OOBE flow, not afterward.
tip: Autopilot user-driven flow: Power on → Internet → Hardware hash identified → Autopilot profile applied → Company branding → User signs in → Azure AD join → Intune enrolment → ESP (policies, apps install) → Desktop ready. Key concept: NO imaging, NO IT touch, cloud-driven. ESP (Enrolment Status Page) blocks the desktop until critical apps/policies are installed.

Scenario:
- Your company uses Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
- The security team wants to:
  - Make Global Administrator assignments time-limited (eligible, not permanent)
  - Require approval before a user can activate the Global Admin role
  - Require MFA when activating the role
  - Send notifications when the role is activated

Question:
Which PIM configuration achieves all of these requirements?
choices: Create a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for Global Admins
Use Azure AD access reviews to review Global Admin assignments monthly
Configure PIM role settings for Global Admin: eligible assignment, require approval, require MFA on activation, enable notifications
Assign the Global Admin role as a permanent active assignment
explanations: Conditional Access can require MFA when a Global Admin signs in, but it doesn't provide: eligible assignments, time-limited access, approval workflows, or activation-specific notifications. Conditional Access is always-on enforcement; PIM is just-in-time governance. They complement each other but serve different purposes.

Access reviews periodically review role assignments and ask 'Should this user still have this role?' They're important for governance hygiene but don't provide real-time activation controls (approval, MFA, time-limits, notifications). Access reviews = periodic cleanup. PIM settings = per-activation governance.

This option is correct. PIM role settings for Global Administrator: (1) Assignment type = Eligible (not Active) — user must activate when needed. (2) Activation maximum duration = time-limited (e.g., 8 hours). (3) Require approval = yes, with designated approvers. (4) Require MFA on activation = yes (user must MFA before the role activates). (5) Notification settings = send email when the role is activated. This implements just-in-time (JIT) privileged access with full governance controls.

Permanent active assignments are the OPPOSITE of what PIM is designed to prevent. PIM's purpose is to eliminate standing (permanent) privileged access. Making Global Admin permanent means the user always has the role — no time limit, no activation, no approval.
tip: PIM role settings per role: eligible vs active assignment, max activation duration, require MFA on activation, require approval (with approvers), require justification, enable notifications. PIM = just-in-time privileged access. Conditional Access = always-on enforcement. Access reviews = periodic role assignment review. All three should work together.
